sources.description: A historical study written in 1949 and published in 1981. Quigley traces elite networks through education, publishing, imperial governance and foreign policy. His appendix labels the membership roster tentative, with possible errors and explicitly bracketed conjectures. The archive distinguishes reported roles from his inferred affiliations. The PDF remains a local research document and is not redistributed by this site.
sources.coverage: All 13 chapters represented by selected records; the tentative appendix roster is indexed. Not every name, date, footnote, or passing reference has been extracted.

sources.description: An Asia-Pacific Journal / Japan Focus article examining the interplay of security institutions, financial elites and international covert operations. Causal arguments and quoted interpretations are attributed to Scott or their named authors; the notes include denials and evidentiary qualifications. The PDF header gives March 3, the recommended citation March 10, and the revision March 13, 2014.
sources.coverage: Article and all endnotes reviewed. Selective extraction of dated events, institutions and people; passing names are not exhaustive.

evidenceIssues.description: Publication header and recommended citation disagree (March 3 versus March 10); explicit update March 13, 2014.
Scott notes establishment writers describe Copeland memoirs as unreliable; claims from Copeland remain attributed.
Nixon briefcase donation story is disputed by Kolb, and Baer gives 1968 rather than 1972; not included as a factual dated event.
Safari Club resort and intelligence alliance are separate entities; Scott presents both official-policy origin and later circumvention interpretations.
Notes 103 and 105 explicitly state no published evidence Copeland was involved in Safari Club covert operations; no membership edge created.
Scott’s oil-boycott interpretation is denied by Exxon corporate history in note 48.
The article’s parenthetical company labels conflate Standard Oil of New York/Socony and California. A collective oil-cartel record avoids reproducing the naming error.
Ownership and job descriptions are historical statements as of the 2014 article, not claims about current roles.

sources.description: Oglesby interprets Dallas, Watergate and the Hughes business struggle through competing elite factions. Alternative assassination, covert-operation and sabotage theories remain source-attributed; denials and official accounts are preserved.

sources.title: Tragedy and Hope: A History of the World in Our Time
sources.author: Carroll Quigley
sources.description: A wide-ranging historical synthesis of financial capitalism, imperial administration, international diplomacy, world wars and the Cold War. This supplied PDF is a retyped, annotated edition rather than a facsimile of the 1966 printing. Accounts distinguish Quigley’s interpretations from the later introduction and visible editorial insertions.
sources.pageConvention: All citations use 1-based pages of this 1,090-page PDF. These are not page numbers in the original Macmillan printing. January 1 and the first of a month are plotting anchors for dates whose day is not given.
sources.coverage: Selective, substantive extraction across the book’s institutional and political chapters, with emphasis on finance, empire and connections through the 1950s; selected 1960s developments extend the chronology. This is not an exhaustive index of every name, battle or theoretical passage. Selected institutional, financial and imperial passages in chapters 5–14 (PDF pages 47–229), with particular attention to banking mechanisms, Rhodes–Milner affiliations, constitutional reforms and the diplomatic origins of the First World War. Civilizational theory and passing references are not exhaustively indexed. Additional selected pages158–186 address foreign customs supervision, Japan’s political-economic organization and Chinese republican instability. Substantial reading of PDF pages 230–307, 399–417, and 449–454 within chapters 15–38, concentrating on the Versailles settlement, collective security, reparations, central-bank cooperation, stabilization and the 1931 crisis, British political institutions and labor, and the New Deal. This is a selective event-and-network digest, not an exhaustive transcription of every country chapter. PDF pages 472–792, chapters 39–65: Japanese and Italian aggression, British appeasement and institutional networks, European war, Allied strategy and postwar institutions, atomic diplomacy, and Cold War formation through 1950. The supplied PDF contains bracketed editorial interpolations; this digest does not attribute those additions to Quigley. Dates retain the precision supported by the supplied text, and known internal date inconsistencies are identified rather than silently repaired. Substantive reading of PDF pages 793–994, covering nuclear strategy, Korea, Eisenhower institutions, Soviet succession, Iran, Suez, Cuba, and Asian/African decolonization; selected late-book analysis pp 1011,1031–1034 and concluding 1963–1964 developments pp 1088–1090. Summaries exclude recognizable bracketed editorial interpolations. Citations use PDF page numbers, not printed-page labels.

evidenceIssues.description: A later introductory essay mentions a 1996 study and advances additional claims. It is not Quigley’s 1966 text and is excluded from Quigley-attributed profiles and events.

The supplied edition contains visible bracketed editorial comments, omissions and editorial-sounding headings. Digests use the body passages, exclude identified editorial insertions and do not attribute the headings’ rhetoric to Quigley.

Some dates conflict within the supplied text: the Oppenheimer passage and Bay of Pigs references require care. Specific event accounts record their citation and precision notes; contradictory passages are not silently reconciled.
